title: Nearcast WebMCP
pitch: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S.
about_excerpt: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S. Like Comment Story Updates Map Overview Focusing on a specific region Human + Agent Shared State Cross-Border Hazard Comparison Inspiration Nearcast began as a Canadian iPhone app that pulls official hazard data. Hazard maps are exactly the kind of interface generic browser agents struggle with: hundreds of clustered markers, a dozen filter combinations, geographic bounds, a selection, and six agencies' worth of heterogeneous records. WebMCP lets the page say what it can do instead of making the agent infer it from the DOM. What it does Nearcast WebMCP shows current wildfires, weather alerts and earthquakes across Canada and the United States on one MapLibre map, normalized from six official sources (ECCC, NRCan CWFIS, Earthquakes Canada, NWS, NIFC, USGS) with explicit attribution and freshness. Every source fails independently; if a feed is down the app says so and keeps working. It exposes eight WebMCP tools that read and mutate the same application state the human is looking at: get_current_view — map bounds, zoom, filters, selected hazard, counts, source freshness get_visible_hazards — concise list of what is on screen after all filters set_focus_area — move the map to regions ( ["BC","WA"] ), bounds, or a point set_hazard_filters — countries, hazard types, minimum weather severity, minimum magnitude focus_hazard — select a hazard exactly like a human click (highlight, pan, details panel) get_hazard_details — full record with agency classifications and the official link compare_regions — deterministic counts for provinces/states create_situation_context — structured facts for an area; the agent writes the prose An Agent Activity panel logs every tool call, so people can see what the agent did. Why WebMCP fits this use case Map applications hold large amounts of visual state. Screen-scraping and clicking is brittle and slow. WebMCP gives the agent typed, described operations while keeping human and agent in the same visible workspace : the human zooms and clicks, the agent reads that through get_current_view , changes filters or focus, and the human sees it happen and refines by hand. Better UX Instead of manually toggling countries, filtering hazard types and scanning hundreds of markers, the user says "Focus on British Columbia and Washington and show only wildfires and important weather alerts" — and still sees and controls the resulting map. Verified live in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with GPT-5.6. What humans and agents do together Human: explores visually, selects incidents, validates context, controls decisions. Agent: manipulates filters, compares regions, retrieves structured details, surfaces relevant information, writes the narrative. Application: authoritative normalized data, deterministic geographic calculations and counts, visual state — and never a "you are safe" claim. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + MapLibre GL (OpenFreeMap basemap, no tokens). One TypeScript Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API with six source adapters ( Promise.allSettled , per-source timeouts, stale-snapshot fallback), a shared hazard model, and severity translation kept alongside raw agency classifications. CloudFront serves the SPA from a private S3 bucket (OAC) and routes /api/* to API Gateway so everything is same-origin; Terraform provisions all of it. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and wrap the app's own store actions — the same functions a click uses. No AI API keys anywhere: WebMCP is the AI integration. Challenges Government feeds are inconsistent: CWFIS's national fire layer is temporal (189k rows; only rows whose validity window includes "now" are current), most NWS alerts have no polygon (placed at Census county centroids and flagged approximate ), Earthquakes Canada is pipe-delimited text. Keeping severity honest: earthquakes and US wildfires have no agency severity, so we expose magnitude/hectares plus a clearly labelled display significance instead of inventing one. Demo robustness: per-source failure handling, stale snapshots, and a clearly labelled demo-data mode. Accomplishments Live cross-border six-source hazard workspace; eight well-described tools; shared state proven by get_current_view reflecting manual pans and clicks; 44 unit tests; reproducible Terraform deployment; verified end-to-end in ChatGPT's built-in browser. What we learned Tool descriptions and strict schemas matter more than tool count. Deterministic, structured outputs (counts, ids, source status) let the agent explain without hallucinating, and a visible activity log makes the collaboration legible to people. What's next Evacuation orders (BC first), air quality, time-windowed regional summaries, and Chrome origin-trial enrollment. Safety Nearcast is an awareness tool, not an emergency service. It always shows the issuing agency, timestamps and the official link, and reminds users to follow local emergency authorities. Built With amazon-api-gateway amazon-cloudfront amazon-web-services aws-lambda maplibre-gl node.js openstreetmap react terraform typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out hazards.securitygeek.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I designed the product and the human + agent experience, chose the government data sources (reusing what I learned building the Nearcast iPhone app), and built and deployed the full stack: React/MapLibre front end, TypeScript Lambda API, Terraform on AWS, and the eight WebMCP tools. I used Claude Code as a pair programmer throughout and tested the tools live in ChatGPT's desktop browser and Chrome. Biggest lesson: good tool descriptions and deterministic, structured outputs matter far more than tool count.
